item.title: Expressive Shallow Networks for Physics-Informed Learning: Why Curvature-Aware Optimization and FP64 Are Not Enough
item.description: arXiv:2611.28393v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) often struggle with high-frequency and high-order partial differential equations (PDEs) due to optimization stiffness and spectral bias, despite possessing sufficient approximation capacity. Existing remedies, including modified feature representations, domain decomposition, higher floating-point precision, and curvature-aware optimizers, can improve convergence but largely act as workarounds for optimization difficulties arising from deep architectures rather than addressing their underlying source. We investigate Physics-Informed Shallow Universal Polynomial Networks (PI-SUPNs), which replace deep nonlinear compositions with learnable polynomial expansions, retaining high approximation capacity within a shallow computational graph. On a high-frequency Helmholtz benchmark, PI-SUPNs are the only architecture to successfully recover the solution, while all competing models fail even under FP64 precision and curvature-aware optimization. However, experiments on higher vibrational modes of a fourth-order Euler-Bernoulli beam reveal that architectural improvements alone are insufficient: accurate solutions require the combination of PI-SUPNs, FP64 precision, and curvature-aware optimization. Additionally, Allen-Cahn experiments show that PI-SUPNs achieve lower solution and derivative errors at reduced computational cost, with more favorable loss landscapes than competing architectures. We also establish quasi-local approximation properties and spline-based convergence bounds for SUPNs. Our results show that shallow network architectures are an important mechanism for improving physics-informed trainability, but accurate solutions to the most challenging PDEs can still require FP64 precision and curvature-aware optimization.
item.dc:creator: Zachary Morrow, Yucheng Fu, Pratanu Roy, Michael Penwarden

item.title: Kinetic versus refill-zone uncertainty in predicted pr--burning of methane-oxygen rotating detonation rocket engines
item.description: arXiv:2611.28404v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rotating detonation rocket engines can lose performance when fresh propellant mixes with hot recirculated combustion products and ignites before the detonation wave arrives. Predicting this pre-burning requires fuel ignition chemistry at high pressure and in product-diluted mixtures, conditions most chemical kinetic mechanisms used in engine simulations were not developed for. With methane as our base fuel, we quantify how strongly predicted pre-burning depends on the choice of mechanism, test the mechanisms against published high-pressure ignition data, and use Bayesian methods to calibrate the most influential uncertain reaction and to assess which measurements would best improve the predictions. As the refill zone is represented by an idealized zero-dimensional model, our results should be viewed as relative comparisons rather than direct engine predictions. Five existing chemical kinetics mechanisms for methane combustion predict refill-zone ignition delays that differ by up to a factor of twenty. Mechanisms without methylperoxy chemistry, including two commonly used in engine simulations, do not reproduce the laboratory data below about 1150 K. Calibrating the CH${_3}$ + HO${_2}$ reaction against these data, while allowing for systematic differences between datasets, increases the relative importance of its chain-terminating channel, consistent with a direct rate measurement. With the data-consistent mechanisms, the remaining kinetic uncertainty in the predicted pre-burnt fraction is, in most cases, several times smaller than the uncertainty arising from the state of the refill zone: the temperature and composition of the recirculated products and the way fresh and burnt gases mix. Improved pre-burning predictions are therefore expected to depend mainly on accurately characterizing the refill zone.
item.dc:creator: Y. Sungtaek Ju

item.title: Machine Learning Electronic Hamiltonian with Long-Range Effects and External Fields
item.description: arXiv:2611.28450v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conventional machine-learning electronic Hamiltonian (MLEH) models rely on a local-environment approximation and can miss the effects of long-range (LR) interactions and external fields. Here, we introduce MLEH-LR, a framework that incorporates these effects into Hamiltonian prediction. Benchmarks across materials with different polarizations and dimensionalities demonstrate substantial improvements in the accuracy of the predicted Hamiltonians and resulting electronic structures. MLEH-LR enables accurate, large-scale, high-throughput electronic-structure calculations, as demonstrated for zigzag boron nitride ribbons under transverse electric fields. These calculations allow us to formulate a quantitative relation describing the joint width and field dependence of the band gap and to reveal the electronic mechanisms underlying its field response. Our work provides an efficient method and tool for studying electronic structure in materials where long-range electrostatics and external fields play an important role.
item.dc:creator: Xueheng Kuang, Ruoyu Wang, Kwangrae Kim, Rongjing Guo, Yiyang Fu, Yuanyue Liu

item.title: Accelerating wave-scattering simulations with learned search directions
item.description: arXiv:2611.28499v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Wave-scattering simulation requires solving a dense boundary-element system for every frequency, incidence and design. Krylov solvers build each search space from scratch, and it grows with problem size. Here we present BEMFormer, a solver that learns to generate search directions across systems of one integral equation and supplies geometry-specific directions through a coarse-grid correction. BEMFormer generalizes to unseen geometries, meshes and excitations, and to acoustic scattering after fine-tuning on eight geometries. It reproduces the measured radar cross-sections of benchmark targets. On a quadcopter with 1.04 million unknowns, 38 times the largest training problem, BEMFormer solves each system 30 times faster than a preconditioned Krylov solver. Both reach a radar cross-section deviation of about 1 dB, comparable to the difference between independent measurements and acceptable for engineering applications. These results show that solving million-unknown scattering problems in minutes is possible when the search space is learned rather than built from scratch.
item.dc:creator: Haoran Sun, Tao Shan, Hongyu Zhou, Rui Guo, Shenheng Xu, Fan Yang, Maokun Li

item.title: JAX-Nano: A GPU-Accelerated Differentiable Phonon Boltzmann Transport Solver for Nanoscale Heat Transfer
item.description: arXiv:2611.28926v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As semiconductor device dimensions approach phonon mean free paths, heat transport enters ballistic and quasi-ballistic regimes where Fourier's law becomes inadequate. The phonon Boltzmann transport equation (BTE) describes these nonequilibrium effects but presents significant computational challenges. This work introduces JAX-Nano, a GPU-accelerated, end-to-end differentiable phonon BTE solver for nanoscale heat transport. The solver integrates steady-state and transient BTE formulations within a unified finite-volume framework, supporting structured and unstructured meshes, mode-resolved transport, phonon scattering, volumetric heat generation, and multiple boundary conditions. Automatic differentiation enables gradient computation with respect to transport properties, boundary conditions, heat-generation rates, and geometric parameters without separately derived adjoint equations. Numerical predictions are validated against analytical solutions and established BTE solvers across diffusive-to-ballistic regimes. Applications to complex three-dimensional geometries are demonstrated using single-fin, double-fin, and arrayed fin field-effect transistor (FinFET) configurations. Gradient-based inverse learning enables single- and multi-parameter identification, including simultaneous recovery of mode-resolved phonon relaxation times and spatially distributed heat-generation rates in steady-state and transient problems. GPU performance and scalability are evaluated with respect to spatial resolution, angular discretization, and phonon bands, including comparisons with an MPI-based BTE solver. JAX-Nano provides a unified computational framework for three-dimensional phonon transport, automatic differentiation, and inverse parameter identification, enabling sensitivity analysis and optimization of nanoscale thermal systems.
item.dc:creator: Bo Zhang, Amy Zhaomei Zhang

item.title: Digital Models of Widely-Used Powder Characterisation Tools and their Application in DEM Calibration Part III: Packing and Flow Testers
item.description: arXiv:2611.29117v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate calibration remains a critical challenge in the field of discrete element method (DEM) simulations. To work towards more standardised and rigorous methods, this research contributes to a growing open-source library of digital models that faithfully replicate powder characterisation instruments. This paper expands that library by developing and validating digital models for two widely used instruments: the GranuFlow flow through an orifice tester and the GranuPack tapped density analyser. These models are designed to replicate the experimental instruments while incorporating computational optimisations to improve efficiency without compromising on accuracy. An example application of the digital models is shown through a calibration case study for two example materials: micro-crystalline cellulose (MCC) and ion exchange resin. The calibrated models show strong agreement with experimental data through cross-validation, yielding a relative percentage error of 0.57\% for the Hausner ratio (the ion exchange resin) and 4.17\% for a Beverloo fitting parameter (MCC). The addition of these validated, open-source models provides the DEM community with further models for more robust, multi-instrument calibration, and potential for more insight into bulk behaviours under different conditions.
item.dc:creator: B. D. Jenkins, A. L. Nicusan, D. Werner, J. P. K. Seville, A. Neveu, G. Lumay, F. Francqui, C. R. K. Windows-Yule

item.title: A shock-fitting approach to high-order simulation of viscous hypersonic flows based on inviscid implicit shock tracking
item.description: arXiv:2611.29564v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work presents a framework for computing viscous, shock-dominated flows at high Mach and Reynolds numbers in which the bow shock is located by inviscid implicit shock tracking and then treated as a boundary of the viscous computation. The high-order implicit shock tracking (HOIST) method is applied to the Euler equations on a coarse, shock-agnostic mesh to produce a shock-aligned mesh and the shock geometry; the elements upstream of the shock are discarded, the post-shock domain is remeshed to resolve the boundary layer, and the compressible Navier-Stokes equations are solved on it with a high-order interior penalty discontinuous Galerkin method, with the post-shock state prescribed along the shock boundary by the oblique shock relations. Because the shock structure is never resolved, the approach requires neither the extreme element compression nor the specialized formulations that fully coupled viscous shock tracking demands at these conditions; the tracking optimization is confined to the coarse inviscid mesh, and the viscous computation involves no mesh unknowns and no additional nonlinear stabilization. The framework is demonstrated on a Mach 10.6 axisymmetric blunt cone, a Mach 17.6 cylinder, and a Mach 5 sphere in three dimensions, with surface pressure and heat flux in good agreement with experimental measurements and reference computations.
item.dc:creator: Huijing Dong, Alexander M. Perez Reyes, Matthew J. Zahr

item.title: Coarse-Grained Description of Stochastic Neutron Transport in Highly Heterogeneous Reactor Media via Non-Local Feller Boundary Functionals
item.description: arXiv:2611.29680v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents a novel hierarchical coarse-graining framework to model non-Markovian neutron transport within the ultra-heterogeneous, multi-phase subcooled nucleate boiling layer of a nuclear reactor core. By applying Feller's subordination theory to continuous-time random walks, microscopic fluid fluctuations and vapor bubble dynamics are rigorously integrated into macroscopic transport operators through the apparatus of Complete Bernstein Functions (CBF). A modified non-local Fick's law is derived using a $P_1$-Legendre polynomial expansion, mapping the fractal porosity and structural phase boundaries into a stochastically renormalized effective diffusion coefficient. The thermodynamic consistency of the model is grounded within Chentsov's statistical manifolds, demonstrating that granular Poisson-like shot noise yields a geometric-exponential family of distributions characterized by a constant negative information curvature. To evaluate operational safety margins under transient conditions, a generalized Lyapunov functional with a quadratic memory kernel is constructed, and a complex decomposition of the transfer function $H(\omega)$ is performed. The resulting analytical limits are parameterized for a WWER-1000 core layout and translated into an engineering computational sequence suitable for implementation in Mathcad Prime 8 to diagnose the onset of Hopf bifurcations and spatial power oscillations.
item.dc:creator: V. V. Ryazanov

item.title: Topological analysis of permeability tensor in anisotropic porous media
item.description: arXiv:2611.29731v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The permeability of an anisotropic porous medium is a tensor whose off-diagonal components, which describe the deflection of the macroscopic flux away from the driving force, are small and change sign under reflections. We ask whether direction-aware topological data analysis can predict the full permeability tensor of three-dimensional porous media directly from their geometry. We introduce two direction-aware topological descriptors for flow problems: a cone-based filtration, adapted from our earlier work on the elastic stiffness tensor, and a throat-scale filtration built on the distance transform of the pore space. Using permeability tensors computed with the lattice Boltzmann method, we compare them with a comprehensive set of non-topological baselines, comprising statistical microstructure descriptors and physics-based permeability estimators. The topological descriptors are most informative for the off-diagonal components, which the baselines capture least well. There the throat-scale filtration alone outperforms every non-topological descriptor set, including the union of all statistical descriptors and physics-based estimators, and adding it to the baselines consistently improves the prediction. We also confirm the approach on real rock data.
item.dc:creator: Rafa{\l} Topolnicki, Pawe{\l} D{\l}otko, Maciej Matyka

item.title: Cyclic changes of frame for designing non-retracing verification cases for numerical interface tracking
item.description: arXiv:2611.30464v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A forward-backward deformation test supplies an exact final interface, but retracing can allow errors from the two halves to cancel. We construct alternative tests by superposing a cyclic change of frame on the same base deformation. The frame returns to its starting pose, preserving the exact final phase and the deformation history up to rigid placement. A small returning translation can keep trajectories close to the retraced ones. A full rotation about a fixed centre or axis gives closed paths with nonzero winding for material labels that stay off that centre or axis. For incompressible base fields the transformed velocity is divergence-free. We construct discretely solenoidal face fluxes for geometric volume-of-fluid advection by circulating the transformed potential. In three TwoPhaseFlow benchmarks, with a shared time grid for each pair, a full-turn frame increased the final cell-average shape discrepancy in all 30 comparisons, with a median factor of 1.50. The fitted convergence exponent decreased in each of the six benchmark-reconstruction comparisons over the tested grids.
item.dc:creator: Dieter Bothe, Tomislav Mari\'c

item.title: Mass-conservative and phase-consistent transport of phase-confined scalars in front tracking
item.description: arXiv:2611.30693v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In front-tracking multiphase-flow simulations, the Lagrangian front defines the interface geometry and phase regions, while phase-confined scalars are transported independently on a fixed Eulerian mesh. This separation can make the scalar inconsistent with the tracked interface: even a conservative high-order scheme smears the scalar across the interface, leaks it into the other phase and distorts near-interface concentrations despite conserving total mass. We present a transport method that maintains consistency between the scalar and the tracked front while preserving global mass conservation. Instead of the cell-averaged concentration, the method transports the phase-averaged concentration, which is smooth across the interface. This concentration is obtained by dividing the cell-averaged concentration by the phase fraction, extended linearly across the interface and advected. The cell-averaged concentration is rebuilt by multiplying the transported concentration by the front's volume-preserving phase fraction. Because this rebuild can alter the total mass, a uniform shift of the phase-averaged concentration restores it. The method is compared with direct transport of the cell-averaged concentration by the same scheme in five three-dimensional cases: three drops (in translation, in a reversible vortex and with a localized source) and a rising bubble with and without dissolved surfactant. In the four cases without surfactant it reduces the error against the exact solution by more than a factor of ten at the finest resolution and converges faster for the drops. In the surfactant-laden bubble, direct transport leaks 5.5-24% of the surfactant into the wake, depending on resolution, whereas the proposed method keeps it in the bubble.
item.dc:creator: Ayman Mazloum, Gabriele Gennari, Fabian Denner, Berend van Wachem

item.title: PFASST-BISICLES: A Parallel-in-Time Ice Sheet Model
item.description: arXiv:2611.28434v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Efficiently simulating ice sheet dynamics on modern computational systems is essential for projecting the response of ice sheets to climate forcing and the resulting contributions to sea level change. On modern computational systems, this demands high levels of parallelism to fully exploit modern architectures. Traditionally, time-dependent simulations like ice sheet models achieve parallelism entirely by distributing the spatial domain, while remaining serial in time, as solutions are marched forward. We present PFASST-BISICLES, which combines the Parallel Full Approximation Scheme in Space and Time (PFASST) with BISICLES ice sheet model to integrate multiple timesteps concurrently. We evaluate numerical agreement and parallel performance using a fully grounded sinusoidal ice stream with adaptive mesh refinement and the MISMIP+ marine ice-sheet benchmark. For the sinusoidal stream, PFASST-BISICLES produces temporal errors approximately an order of magnitude smaller than forward Euler at the same timestep, although both methods exhibit approximately first-order convergence. Spatial scaling levels off near 16 processors, while temporal parallelism provides further acceleration, with nearly linear speedup through approximately 16 temporal processors. In MISMIP+, PFASST-BISICLES reproduces the main thickness and velocity patterns after glacier evolution of 50 years, with the largest differences concentrated near the grounding zone. Increasing the temporal processor count from one to four, with four spatial processors fixed, reduces runtime from 33.8 to 10.5 hours. These results demonstrate that temporal parallelism can complement spatial decomposition in ice-sheet modeling, reducing time to solution while maintaining agreement in the main simulated features.
item.dc:creator: Weijia (Emma), Liu, Hans Johansen, Daniel F. Martin

item.title: An equivariant classical density functional for ionic fluids at complex interfaces
item.description: arXiv:2611.28501v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Predicting the combined effects of ionic packing and long-range electrostatics at complex interfaces is technologically important, but remains challenging without atomistic simulations. Here we present a machine-learned classical density functional for ionic fluids that combines a symmetry-adapted neural free energy for short-range correlations with explicit long-range electrostatics. Trained on three-dimensional equilibrium densities and bulk correlations of the full-Coulomb restricted primitive model, a single functional transfers to charge-patterned particles and atomically structured electrodes. Around anisotropic charged solutes, it reproduces the ionic structure and mean forces from molecular dynamics, including reversals of the bare electrostatic force. At metal electrodes, self-consistent coupling to metal atoms captures the redistribution of ionic and electrode charge and the loading-dependent capacitance enhancement produced by steps and bumps. Combined with mobilities determined independently from bulk molecular dynamics, the same functional describes the main features of charging dynamics and resolves geometry-dependent spatial relaxation. This framework can be extended to more complex ionic fluids, enabling efficient exploration of how composition and geometry control structure and response.
item.dc:creator: Bingqing Cheng

item.title: Interstitial Magnetoelectricity in Altermagnetic Electrides
item.description: arXiv:2611.28504v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Electrides and altermagnets are two distinct yet intriguing classes of quantum materials, characterized by interstitial anionic electrons and nonrelativistic spin splitting, respectively. The recent prediction of Stoner-instability-driven altermagnetic electride provides a natural bridge between these two fields. Here, we investigate the magnetoelectric response and its related spin-polarized transport in the altermagnetic electride Zr$_2$N monolayer. Using the tight-binding Hubbard model and first-principles calculations, we find that the electric field can break the magnetic compensation between the two interstitial anionic electrons, inducing a finite net magnetization and giving rise to an interstitial electron mediated magnetoelectric response. The magnetoelectric response is further demonstrated through the electrical control of spin conductivity. Our results reveal a magnetoelectric effect in altermagnetic electrides, paving a way towards electride-based spintronic devices.
item.dc:creator: Yue Li, Shibo Fang, Jianhua Wang, Qiang Li, Weizhen Meng, Haiyu Meng, Xiong-Xiong Xue, Jianfeng Wang, Yi Du, Jing Lu, Yee Sin Ang

item.title: LayerCake v1.0: a framework for low- to intermediate-order automated models development
item.description: arXiv:2611.28647v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A new model development framework called LayerCake is presented. It is written in the Python language and relies on the Sympy symbolic computation package to compute the Galerkin projection of two-dimensional spatially extended geophysical models. These projections provide their time evolution operator in the spectral space on a restricted set of modes. The resulting tendencies of the models can be evaluated either numerically (for time integration) or symbolically (for parameters sensitivity analysis and bifurcation analysis). We provide several simple examples of geophysical models to showcase the capabilities of the framework, and we hint at how more complex systems can be designed.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Demaeyer, Ois\'in Hamilton, St\'ephane Vannitsem

item.title: Learning free energy across a differentiable temperature range by deep generative modeling
item.description: arXiv:2611.28810v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Free energy governs the directionality, stability, and temperature sensitivity of physical, chemical, and biological transformations. Conventional free energy calculations, such as thermodynamic integration and free energy perturbation, often have to be performed at individual temperatures and are limited by the high cost of sampling an extensive set of thermodynamic states. Here, we introduce learned temperature-differentiable free energy perturbation (TD-FEP), a deep generative framework that learns a temperature-conditioned, invertible mapping between reference and target systems through data-free, energy-based optimization. TD-FEP thereby unifies one-shot state generation and free energy calculation across a continuous temperature range. We validated TD-FEP across a broad range of applications, including isolated molecules, periodic materials, and chemical reactions.
item.dc:creator: Yaowen Zhang, Chen Chen, Wanyu Lin, Shuo-Hui Li, Ding Pan

item.title: Data handling, production, and simulation in the Muon g-2 Experiment at Fermilab
item.description: arXiv:2611.28851v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper details the computing strategies of the Muon g-2 Experiment at Fermilab, which measured the muon's anomalous magnetic moment with a precision of 127 ppb by processing over 10 petabytes of detector and simulation data. This paper discusses the computational and operational challenges of data production, data handling, and data analysis of such large datasets. These challenges were overcome by using Fermilab-developed software infrastructure and production tools, making efficient use of resources, and improving the collaboration-developed reconstruction workflow. By overcoming these challenges, the experiment improved the data throughput capacity and reduced the analysis turnaround time by an order of magnitude over the course of its lifetime.

item.title: Single-Shot Single-Stage Stellarators
item.description: arXiv:2611.29090v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In stellarator design, the plasma and the coils are so geometrically complex that they are usually designed separately, so that a high-performance plasma may be impossible to reproduce with coils that can actually be manufactured and assembled. We present a new method to close this gap. In this framework, the plasma shape is optimized while, for every candidate shape, near-optimal coils that satisfy hard engineering limits are found. Without any manually-tuned weights, the method steers the plasma towards shapes that real coils can produce. Moreover, we demonstrate the first single-shot optimization runs starting from tokamak ``cold-starts''. From a single-shot cold-start, we design a finite-$\beta$ stellarator comparable to reactor-scaled NCSX, as well as a compact aspect-ratio 2.5 and $\langle\beta\rangle=2\%$ quasi-axisymmetric stellarator with one field period and self-consistent bootstrap current. Starting from a boundary derived from W7-X, we design a quasi-isodynamic stellarator with reactor-relevant stability properties. We then use this to warm-start an optimization for a single coil-set solution that produces a high-performance QI stellarator at every pressure value from vacuum to $\langle\beta\rangle=4\%$, addressing directly the ``start-up'' phase of a reactor. The self-consistent free-boundary solutions for these stellarators typically have better coils than a traditional separate-design approach, at comparable or better plasma performance, illustrating that robust single-stage methods are possible and providing a direct route to the design of reactor-scale stellarators.
item.dc:creator: Pedro F. Gil, Lanke Fu, Alan A. Kaptanoglu

item.title: CLFF: Automated Framework for Concurrent Learning Force Fields and Material Property Calculations
item.description: arXiv:2611.29187v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) offer an efficient paradigm for large-scale atomistic simulations with near first-principles accuracy. However, developing and deploying these potentials often involves intricate procedures that require substantial manual effort and domain expertise. In this work, we present CLFF, an open-source Python framework designed to automate concurrent learning workflows for MLIPs. CLFF integrates model training, MLIP-driven sampling, uncertainty-based candidate selection, quantum-mechanical labeling, and dataset augmentation into a unified workflow. The framework currently supports several modern graph-based MLIP architectures and is compatible with widely used computational chemistry and materials science tools. A distinguishing feature of CLFF is its ability to asynchronously distribute computational tasks across multiple heterogeneous remote computing resources, enabling users to aggregate fragmented hardware infrastructure within a single controllable workflow. In addition to concurrent learning, CLFF provides automated workflows for initial data generation and material property calculations, including phonon dispersion and potential energy surface scans. By minimizing manual intervention and enhancing reproducibility, CLFF offers a flexible platform for developing and deploying MLIPs in computational materials research.
item.dc:creator: Cao Thang Nguyen, Sung Youb Kim

item.title: Nonempirical Determination of the Optimal TAO-DFT Fictitious Temperature for Molecular Systems in the Lowest Singlet State
item.description: arXiv:2611.29414v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Thermally-assisted-occupation density functional theory (TAO-DFT) [J.-D. Chai, J. Chem. Phys., 2012, ${\bf 136}$, 154104] has been developed to investigate the ground-state properties of large electronic systems exhibiting varying multi-reference (MR) character. As a central parameter in TAO-DFT, the fictitious temperature $\theta$ is closely linked to the degree of static correlation in an electronic system. While the conventional system-independent $\theta$-scheme is computationally efficient and broadly applicable, a fixed, preassigned $\theta$ can be overly large for single-reference (SR) systems yet too small for strongly MR systems. To overcome this limitation, we propose a nonempirical scheme based on spin-symmetry restoration to determine the optimal system-dependent fictitious temperature $\theta^{*}$ for molecular systems in their lowest singlet states. Across benchmark tests encompassing both MR systems (the bond dissociation of H$_{2}$, N$_{2}$, Li$_{2}$, and LiH, as well as the torsional rotation of twisted ethylene) and pure SR systems (the dissociation of He$_{2}$ and Ne$_{2}$), our nonempirical approach demonstrates superior overall accuracy compared with the conventional fixed-$\theta$ scheme. Furthermore, relative to standard Kohn-Sham density functional theory (TAO-DFT with $\theta = 0$), TAO-DFT employing $\theta^{*}$ yields substantial improvements for MR systems while preserving comparable accuracy in SR systems.
item.dc:creator: Bing-Ying Li, Jeng-Da Chai

item.title: RxnScope: Accurate joint generation of product and transition-state pairs from reactants via flow matching
item.description: arXiv:2611.29492v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reaction networks are central to understanding chemical reactivity and guiding reaction design. Constructing them when products are unknown remains a major challenge in computational chemistry, requiring the identification of products and their corresponding transition states (TSs) across elementary steps. Here, we introduce RxnScope, a flow-matching framework that jointly generates paired product-TS geometries from reactants, conditioned on a potentially reactive region. Directed product-to-TS coupling allows evolving rather than fixed product geometries to guide TS generation, while paired outputs enable product-topology ranking to prioritize candidates for validation. RxnScope recovered and validated 95.8% of reference pathways on Transition1x, performed robustly on multicomponent reactions and enabled multistep pathway exploration. In automatic reaction discovery, it achieved low-energy pathway coverage comparable to that of the single-ended growing string method while using only about 2% of its computational cost. These results establish joint product-TS generation as a new strategy for exploring reaction networks from reactants.
item.dc:creator: Yanyang Li, DaoJing Li, Manyi Yang, Shuhua Li

item.title: AmorphGen: A Python package for amorphous structure generation with machine-learning and classical interatomic potentials
item.description: arXiv:2611.29539v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AmorphGen is an open-source Python package for generating and analyzing amorphous structures from a composition or a crystal. Chemically informed rules estimate initial densities and assign separation and coordination constraints. Three routes are available: random placement followed by relaxation, melt-quench from a crystal, and a hybrid route that anneals and quenches random structures. ASE provides access to classical and machine-learning potentials, with GPU batching for selected backends. Analysis tools compute coordination numbers, bond angles, rings, and X-ray or neutron structure factors for comparison with measurements. An optional interface to the FEFF code computes extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) spectra. For amorphous Ga2O3, TiO2 and InGaZnO4, the cation coordination numbers are close to reference models and measurements, and the X-ray structure factors reproduce the main measured peaks. The EXAFS spectra for Ga2O3 and InGaZnO4 also capture the dominant first-shell features observed experimentally. The hybrid route reduces bonding defects in SiO2 and As and builds the first sharp diffraction peak of SiO2. By simplifying ensemble generation and standardizing structural assessment, AmorphGen makes it practical to compare amorphous models across compositions, potentials, and preparation routes, and to screen new amorphous compositions.
item.dc:creator: Chaiyawat Kaewmeechai, Louie Slocombe, Alexis G. Manche, David O. Scanlon

item.title: MagPot: A magnetoelastic potential generator for molecular dynamics simulations
item.description: arXiv:2611.29574v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Magnetoelastic phenomena originate from the coupling between atomic displacements and magnetic degrees of freedom, and their atomistic simulation requires interatomic models in which magnetic interactions depend explicitly on interatomic distance. This paper presents MagPot, a Python program that generates Bethe-Slater parameter sets for spin-lattice molecular dynamics simulations using the SPIN package of the Large-scale Atomic/Molecular Massively Parallel Simulator (LAMMPS). From a compact set of material properties, the program determines the radial functions describing Heisenberg exchange and the dipole and quadrupole contributions of the two-ion N\'eel interaction. Version 1.0 supports simple-cubic, body-centred-cubic and face-centred-cubic lattices with ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic configurations. A central feature of MagPot is its modular architecture, which allows the magnetic contribution it generates to be combined additively with a broad range of compatible non-magnetic interatomic potentials. The parameterisation workflow is assessed through equation-of-state, Curie-temperature, volume-magnetostriction, pressure-dependent magnetocrystalline-anisotropy and anisotropic-magnetoelastic tests. By automating the construction of the magnetic contribution to the interatomic model, MagPot offers a straightforward and reproducible route from material properties to LAMMPS-ready magnetic interactions, facilitating large-scale atomistic simulations of magnetoelasticity and magnetostriction, as well as physical phenomena associated with magnon-phonon coupling.
item.dc:creator: P. Nieves, I. Korniienko, S. Arapan, A. Fraile, R. Iglesias, D. Legut

item.title: Beyond PINNs: Boundary-Enriched Holomorphic Networks for Laplace Problems
item.description: arXiv:2611.29922v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) solve partial differential equations by penalizing their residual, but this formulation can be difficult to optimize for solutions with singular behaviour. We focus specifically on the two-dimensional Laplace equation, whose strong analytical structure allows the governing equation to be enforced directly in the neural representation. We compare a hybrid harmonic-neural model with a holomorphic neural network whose output is harmonic by construction and therefore requires only boundary training. We further enrich the holomorphic model with singular functions chosen according to the interior angle and boundary conditions at each junction of boundary segments. On six singular benchmarks, the enriched model is the most accurate of the neural models we compare. On the four with a closed-form solution, however, that solution lies in the span of the enrichment terms, and a least-squares fit of these terms alone is exact to rounding error. On Motz's problem and the cracked beam, the neural core reduces the relative error of the recovered leading singular coefficient from about $10^{-2}$, for a least-squares fit with the same four terms, to about $10^{-6}$, and on four variants whose solution has a smooth part outside the span, the network is $4\times10^{4}$ to $2\times10^{7}$ times more accurate than a fit of its singular terms alone; classical least-squares fits with more singular terms, or with harmonic polynomials and rational poles, are more accurate still. Our results demonstrate how exploiting problem-specific analytical structure can provide an alternative to base and residual PINNs for challenging scientific computing problems.
item.dc:creator: Andrei Vlad Nicula, Kalp Shah, Robert-Stefan Sofroni, Mihnea Andrei B\^arsan, Agneya Bhardwaj, Jan Jel\'inek, Chris Hoes, Remco Hogerwerf, Finn Govers, Storm Koper, Gerrit Janssen, Stef de Wildt, Alejandro Valverde Mahou

item.title: Scalable Modal Analysis of the Imperial Front Wing Flow Field
item.description: arXiv:2611.29995v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The aerodynamic performance of motorsport vehicles relies on understanding the unsteady flow dynamics around complex geometries at high Reynolds numbers. Extracting the dominant 3D coherent structures from high-fidelity simulations is often intractable due to the high dimensionality of the state-space, and standard modal decompositions, such as proper orthogonal decomposition (POD), do not give interpretable meaning to the temporal dynamics of the modes. This study demonstrates a scalable POD and Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) method, implemented in the open-source pyLOM framework, that can identify coherent structures and their temporal dynamics in high-fidelity simulations of Formula 1 aerodynamics, specifically the Imperial Front Wing (IFW), a publicly available benchmark based on the McLaren MP4-17D, at Reynolds number $Re = 2.2 \times 10^5$. DMD is applied to large eddy simulation (LES) results of the flow field that is resolved using spectral/hp element method via Nektar++, producing $49.72 \times 10^6$ degrees of freedom at polynomial order p=4. The simulation captures four dominant vortical structures (endplate, canard, main, and footplate), with time-averaged force coefficients showing 2.24% and 2.87% differences in $C_L$ and $C_D$ compared to the reference data. DMD extracts the frequencies, amplitudes and damping ratios of the coherent structures, and modes at chord-based Strouhal numbers of 5.1, 7.5 and 9.3 are associated, through point-probe spectra, with the main-element laminar separation bubble, canard vortex core pulsation and endplate vortex meander, respectively. The DMD allows for both a model reduction technique and a compression scheme, here reducing approximately 6 TB of snapshots to 200 GB of modal data.
item.dc:creator: Parv Khurana, Benet Eiximeno, Alexandra Liosi, Spencer Sherwin, Athanasios Chatzopoulos, Julien Hoessler, Arnau Mir\'o, Oriol Lehmkuhl, Ivette Rodriguez, J. Nathan Kutz

item.title: A Unified Energy-Density Framework for Moir\'e Interface Energetics and Mechanics
item.description: arXiv:2611.30152v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The mechanical response of moir\'e interfaces depends on how atomic registry combines with contact size and boundary geometry. An analytical description must retain this discrete lattice information while connecting microscopic interactions to the energetics of finite contacts. Here, we develop a unified energy-density framework for rigid van der Waals interfaces by expressing registry-dependent pair potentials and atomic densities in reciprocal space. The resulting formulation accommodates different lattice bases and atomic species, linking single-atom and molecular adsorption to infinite bilayers and finite crystalline contacts. Explicit expressions for circular and regular polygonal flakes separate the area contribution from boundary-dependent terms and connect microscopic corrugation coefficients to energy barriers, rotational torques, and interlayer shear stiffnesses. The boundary analysis recovers the quarter-power area scaling of the barrier envelope for circular flakes and distinguishes bounded oscillations from square-root area scaling for polygonal contacts according to edge orientation. A dimensionless criterion characterizes the polygon-to-circle crossover in terms of moir\'e wavelength, flake size, and side number. Direct-summation benchmarks support the finite-domain expressions, while calculations for two-dimensional ice on graphene demonstrate the corresponding boundary-scaling trends in a molecular lattice. Applications to interlayer shear and graphite compression connect the same microscopic interaction description to tangential and normal mechanical responses. The framework establishes an analytical connection between microscopic registry, moir\'e periodicity, and finite-domain geometry, providing a basis for understanding and tailoring the energetics and mechanics of van der Waals contacts.
item.dc:creator: Zhangke Lei, Weidong Yan, Zhicheng Feng, Wengen Ouyang

item.title: Growing Knot Embeddings into Spherical Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2611.30245v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Knotted structures occur throughout soft matter and biology, where topological constraints can shape relaxation and spatial organization. Here, we introduce a computational construction that maps a specific 3D knot embedding to a graph embedded on the sphere through growth and interfacial-energy relaxation. For standard 3D embeddings of prime knots with at most seven crossings, we obtain a family of growth-based graphs that generally differ from the corresponding Tait graphs. We further identify an empirical growth-graph reconstruction rule based on polygonal regions with alternating crossing structure in a knot diagram. Non-minimal diagrams demonstrate that these graphs are not knot invariants, while selected connected sums suggest that graph features associated with their prime factors can remain recognizable. Determining how these graphs transform under isotopy may reveal invariant features, which we leave for future study.
item.dc:creator: Eren G\"ulmez, Joost de Graaf

item.title: SPECTRA-RCWA: A Spectral Propagation Engine for Coupled-Wave Theory with Recursive Admittance
item.description: arXiv:2611.30305v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Rigorous coupled-wave analysis (RCWA) is the standard full-wave solver for periodic metasurfaces, but every solve diagonalises a dense nonsymmetric matrix for each layer. Inverse design repeats this step for every wavelength, angle and polarisation of an objective. On a graphics processor it is the slow step, and its derivative fails where eigenvalues coincide or a diffraction order reaches cutoff. Here we introduce SPECTRA-RCWA, an RCWA forward and adjoint solver that never diagonalises the layer matrix. Each layer step uses three entire functions of the half-size layer matrix, evaluated by matrix products alone, and an admittance recursion, or scattering-matrix doubling for thick layers, keeps the evanescent orders stable. One adjoint field gives the gradient for every design value without a computational graph, and all solves of an objective run as one batch. For 144 solves with 578 x 578 layer matrices, the value and the gradient take 0.25 s on one graphics card, 218 times less than with a differentiable eigendecomposition code. The truncated-series solver TorchRDIT loses accuracy beyond a few tenths of a micrometre unless the user slices the layer; SPECTRA-RCWA keeps single-precision accuracy in layers several wavelengths thick with no setting changed and is 47 to 65 times faster at matched accuracy. Its single-precision gradient stays within 4e-5 of a double-precision reference at a cutoff, where eigendecomposition gradients are wrong by order one. A freeform metagrating designed in 3.4 min on a desktop processor deflects both polarisations by 65 degrees with a band-averaged efficiency of 75%.
item.dc:creator: Hyoseok Park

item.title: Atomistic insight into defect-mediated boron redistribution and high-temperature strengthening in TiAl alloys
item.description: arXiv:2611.30330v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Boron (B) microalloying can effectively refine microstructures of as-cast TiAl alloys and regulate their mechanical properties. Yet, how dilute B exists in TiAl and interacts with defects and how these interactions govern high-temperature deformation remain elusive. Here, we systematically elucidate defect-mediated B redistribution in TiAl alloys and its consequences for their deformation using hybrid grand-canonical Monte Carlo/molecular dynamics simulations augmented with a newly developed high-fidelity machine-learning potential. As a typical product of B microalloying, borides are markedly stiffer than the TiAl matrix and act as brittle reinforcing phases, while borides/matrix interfacial adhesion depends on surface termination and stacking sequence. In the bulk, interstitial B tends to be trapped at Ti-rich octahedral sites by high migration barriers but can kinetically evolve into substitutional dopants upon approaching Al vacancies. Increased tensile stress and vacancy concentration further promote B enrichment in the bulk. B is enriched at semi-coherent $\gamma/\alpha_2$ boundaries and preferentially partitions into the $\alpha_2$ phase. In polycrystalline TiAl, B accumulates primarily in disordered regions, raising the average flow stress by 9.4% at 1 at.% B and 900 K. This strengthening is accompanied by reduced shear strain accumulation. Simulated microstructural evolution and stacking-fault energetics indicate that B impedes dislocation glide via local pinning and suppresses deformation twinning, thereby increasing resistance to plastic deformation. By linking solute redistribution to defect interactions and deformation, these findings establish an atomistic framework for understanding and designing high-performance alloys based on interstitial solutes.
item.dc:creator: Xiang Meng, Shuhei Shinzato, Zhiqiang Zhao, Linfeng Yu, Jian Guo, Liangli Chu, Kepeng Ouyang, Shigenobu Ogata, Zhuhua Zhang

item.title: High-Throughput Screening of Phononic Bandgap in Experimentally Realized Materials
item.description: arXiv:2611.30344v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Materials with a phonon band gap offer a unique mechanism to restrict phonon scattering, making them promising candidates for developing functional materials for targeted thermal applications. Unlocking this mechanism across broad material classes requires systematic exploration, but first-principles methods and experiments are too expensive. Here, we used the universal machine-learning interatomic potential to quantify phonons and thermodynamic properties. We validated the accuracy of machine-learning-calculated results by comparing them with density-functional theory. We screened 154,879 materials and performed phonon calculations for 42,347 thermodynamically stable and experimentally observed compounds. We then performed phonon band gap analysis for dynamically stable materials and identified 11,176 materials with a phononic gap, including 10,960 materials with optical-optical gaps and 270 with acoustic-optical gaps. We also analyzed the lattice thermal conductivity of materials with phonon band gaps to identify candidates with acoustic-optical gaps and low thermal conductivity. Finally, by solving the linearized phonon Boltzmann equation from first principles, we demonstrate low room-temperature lattice thermal conductivities in three Li-metal binaries.
item.dc:creator: Mohammad Bagheri, Kameyab Raza Abidi, Pekka Koskinen

item.title: A new frequency-time hybrid RPML-BIE solver with few-mode corrections for the wave-equation problems in nonuniform closed waveguides
item.description: arXiv:2611.30579v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper is devoted to proposing a novel FTH integral equation solver for wave-equation problems in two-dimensional nonuniform closed waveguides with multiple channels. The FTH methodology, which combines the Fourier transform with frequency-domain BIE formulations, has demonstrated its effectiveness in solving time-dependent wave scattering problems. However, when applied to waveguide problems, the modal expansions arising from multiple scattering introduce cut-off frequencies. Such frequencies pose significant challenges, requiring both a frequency-robust solver for frequency-domain waveguide problems and an efficient treatment of the solution's non-smooth behavior near the cut-off frequencies for the evaluation of the inverse Fourier transform. The first issue is addressed by developing a new frequency-domain BIE method based on the free-space fundamental solution and regionalized perfectly matched layer truncation, together with a few-mode Dirichlet-to-Robin modification. The method is rigorously proved to achieve uniform exponential convergence, even at frequencies arbitrarily close to the cut-off frequencies. To address the second issue---the recovery of the time-domain solution via the inverse Fourier transform---a sine-transform based stationary-point Filon--Clenshaw--Curtis quadrature is introduced to accurately handle the non-smoothness and square-root singularities of frequency-domain solutions. Additionally, theoretical result shows that the complex resonances closing to the real axis may significantly effect the convergence of the Fourier transform algorithm and then a novel strategy of complex resonance extraction based on AAA rational approximation and singularity subtraction is utilized to avoid this influence. Numerical experiments for both frequency-domain and time-domain problems illustrate the efficiency and high accuracy of the proposed method.
item.dc:creator: Yan Tan, Liwei Xu, Tao Yin

item.title: Geometry-conditioned differentiable surrogate with adjoint Monte Carlo sampling for scintillator detector co-design
item.description: arXiv:2611.30580v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Optimizing light-guide geometries for scintillator-based imaging detectors requires repeated photon-transport evaluations, making direct Monte Carlo simulation computationally costly. Differentiable surrogates can accelerate these evaluations and support detector readout co-design aimed at improving information extraction from particle interactions. In this work we describe a surrogate model for photon transport. We develop it starting from a modular, event-driven Monte Carlo model for the generation and transport of scintillation photons, and a reciprocal Monte Carlo construction (an adjoint model) of a spatially and temporally resolved optical response field. The latter evaluates the collectible light output and its temporal structure from a scintillator volume by launching weighted photon trajectories from the light-guide readout face. We apply this approach to a scintillator cell with two mirrored, curved, single-clad light guides. We employ the adjoint model to train a geometry-conditioned neural surrogate that predicts collection probabilities and conditional transport-time distributions across a constrained guide-design family. The surrogate is natively differentiable, lending itself to be an element of a differentiable pipeline for gradient-based optimization. A forward-reciprocal benchmark and validation on held-out geometries establish the accuracy of the trained model and identify its limitations. The developed tools provide a foundation for rapid optical-response studies and detector readout co-design.
item.dc:creator: Lorenzo Pepa, Mohammad Ali Marashli, Nicolas Babio Elguero, Tommaso Dorigo, Irene Fagnani, Carlo Gulizia, Pablo Martinez Ruiz del Arbol, Fredrik Sandin, Pietro Vischia

item.title: A particle method for the space homogeneous Lenard-Balescu equation
item.description: arXiv:2611.30808v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We propose a structure preserving particle method to numerically approximate the spatially homogeneous Lenard-Balescu equation for collisional plasmas. The Lenard-Balescu operator is an improvement of the Landau equation with a dielectric function taking the dynamic screening effect into account. Our particle method is based on the variational formulation of the Lenard-Balescu equation under suitable regularization analogous to the strategy followed for the Landau collision operator in [12]. The method guarantees the conservation laws and the entropy dissipation at the semi-discrete level. The novel difficulty of the nonlocal nonlinear dependence of the dielectric function is tackled by rewriting it as integrals in terms of orthogonal and parallel components to the frequency variable. This equivalent form reduces the evaluation of the dielectric function to numerically computing an integral of the directional derivative of the solution on a hyperplane orthogonal to the frequency variable and its one-dimensional Hilbert transform. An efficient implementation of the numerical approximation for the Lenard-Balescu kernel is derived by exploiting this expression of the dielectric function. We finally validate our method by means of several numerical tests, further allowing us to explore qualitative properties of the Lenard-Balescu equation.
item.dc:creator: Jos\'e Antonio Carrillo, Timon Gutleb, Andrea Medaglia, Yijia Tang

item.title: Lincege.jl: LINked Cluster Expansions on a GEneral GEometry
item.description: arXiv:2611.31102v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The numerical linked-cluster expansion (NLCE) is a powerful tool for studying properties of quantum lattice models directly in the thermodynamic limit. Here, we introduce Lincege.jl, a versatile, efficient, and easy-to-use package for generating the clusters needed to perform the NLCE on a general finite or infinite lattice. Lincege.jl takes as input only the Bravais lattice vectors, the basis information, and the expansion unit and uses a depth-first search to efficiently generate clusters, their lattice constants, and the sub-cluster information. It outputs final coefficients of the series, expressed in terms of the extensive properties of the clusters, in different orders. The package also contains tools for visualizing the lattice and the generated clusters as well as a classical Ising model solver that can be used as a template for interfacing Lincege.jl with solvers of other lattice models. This package can be installed using the Julia package manager and utilized with example scripts from our GitHub repository at https://github.com/rightleftspin/Lincege.jl. The online documentation, including examples, can be found at https://rightleftspin.github.io/Lincege.jl/stable/.
item.dc:creator: Pranav Seetharaman, Francisco Correia, Ehsan Khatami

item.title: Towards Higher Order Oscillatory Ising Machines
item.description: arXiv:2504.18486v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Ising machines as hardware solvers of combinatorial optimization problems (COPs) can efficiently explore large solution spaces due to their inherent parallelism and physics-based dynamics. Many important COP classes such as satisfiability (SAT) assume arbitrary interactions between problem variables, while most Ising machines only support pairwise (second-order) interactions. This necessitates translation of higher-order interactions to pair-wise, which typically results in extra variables not corresponding to problem variables, and a larger problem for the Ising machine to solve than the original problem. This in turn can significantly increase time-to-solution and/or degrade solution accuracy. In this paper, considering a representative CMOS-compatible class of Ising machines, we propose a practical design to enable direct hardware support for higher order interactions. By minimizing the overhead of problem translation and mapping, our design leads to up to 4x lower time-to-solution without compromising solution accuracy.
item.dc:creator: Nafisa Sadaf Prova, H\"usrev C{\i}lasun, Abhimanyu Kumar, Ahmet Efe, Sachin S. Sapatnekar, Ulya R. Karpuzcu

item.title: Dictionary learning approach to analytic continuation of imaginary-time quantum Monte Carlo data
item.description: arXiv:2606.19205v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many fields of physics use quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) simulations to simulate quantum systems in imaginary-time $\tau$ and estimate imaginary-time correlation functions (ITCF). However, extracting dynamic $\omega$-dependent quantities from ITCFs is a notoriously difficult task, known as analytic continuation (AC), that amounts to solving an exponentially ill-conditioned inverse problem. Within the AC literature, there are competing stochastic and regularized approaches, as well as an emerging collection of works using parameterized models like neural networks. Here we transcend the traditional divides between the communities, introducing the regularized stochastic optimization method (RSOM). This method reformulates AC as a dictionary learning problem, discovering a sparse dictionary to represent the solution. Our approach is motivated by the astounding results dictionary learning has produced in many scientific fields. Remarkably, RSOM discovers a sparse dictionary that maps a high-dimensional ill-conditioned inverse problem to a low-dimensional problem. We demonstrate that the method yields competitive results for common synthetic test problems as well as for authentic QMC data from the finite temperature electron gas. Due to the low dimensionality, there is reasonably finite uncertainty in the dictionary, which is leveraged to create an \textit{ad hoc} post-processing estimate of the dictionary coefficients' sensitivity to perturbations. This work exposes that a dictionary exists within all stochastic and regularized methods and that dictionary learning provides a new angle of attack for future AC methods.
item.dc:creator: Thomas Chuna, Phil-Alexander Hofmann, Alexander Benedix-Robles, Tobias Dornheim

item.title: High-fidelity simulation and reduced-order modeling of optical pumping in quantum devices
item.description: arXiv:2610.41778v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Predicting spin polarization and light attenuation in optically pumped atomic devices requires solving the coupled diffusive quantum master equation (DQME)--light system. Its nonlinearity, spatially nonlocal coupling, and physical admissibility constraints make high-fidelity numerical simulation challenging. We develop a structure-preserving high-fidelity solver that combines second-order finite differences for three-dimensional atomic diffusion, explicit pseudo-time marching for atomic populations, and an exponential integrator for light propagation. Under a derived time-step restriction, the solver preserves population normalization and nonnegativity, as well as the positivity and monotonic attenuation of the light intensity. Three complementary test cases based on an analytical reduction, asymptotic limits, and an analytical invariant are constructed to verify the solver. To accelerate repeated parameter queries, we eliminate the light field and construct a reduced-order model (ROM) using proper orthogonal decomposition and Galerkin projection of the resulting integro-differential formulation involving only atomic populations. An exact quadratic expansion of the spin-exchange term and discrete empirical interpolation of the optical-pumping term make the cost of evaluating the reduced operators independent of the full-order dimension. Numerical tests verify the solver and demonstrate ROM accuracy outside the training set. The GPU implementation completes simulations with millions of unknowns in minutes, while single-core ROM evaluations take seconds, achieving respective speedup factors exceeding 150 and 7000 relative to the single-core high-fidelity solver.
item.dc:creator: Keyu Xu, Kezheng Yan, Jinbo Hu, Yanqing Shi, Xiaorui Xu, Nan Zhao, Qian Wang

item.title: The state of nuclear data for fusion activation simulations
item.description: arXiv:2611.24653v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This report compares decay-heat calculations made with four nuclear data libraries, TENDL-2025, ENDF/B-VIII.1, JEFF-4.0 and JENDL-5, against the JAEA FNS decay-heat benchmark. The main comparison uses the 2000 campaign, in which 73 foils were irradiated for five minutes in a mostly 14 MeV neutron field and their decay heat was measured for about an hour. The 1996 seven-hour campaign, with 29 foils and cooling times of up to 400 days, is compared separately and is not included in the rankings. Over the 69 elemental foils solved by all four libraries, the median deviation from the measurement (the mean absolute C/E deviation of each foil) is JENDL-5 17 percent, TENDL-2025 19 percent, JEFF-4.0 22 percent and ENDF/B-VIII.1 44 percent. No library is best everywhere: JENDL-5 on 24, JEFF-4.0 on 18, TENDL-2025 on 17 and ENDF/B-VIII.1 on 10 of the foils. For each element the report breaks the heat down by product and lists the nuclear data on which the libraries differ, and the final sections propose measurements, including enriched-isotope irradiations, that would resolve the largest differences.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Shimwell

item.title: A Semi-Lagrangian Adaptive Rank (SLAR) Method for High-Dimensional Vlasov Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2510.24861v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We extend our previous work on a semi-Lagrangian adaptive rank (SLAR) integrator, in the finite difference framework for nonlinear Vlasov-Poisson systems, to the general high-order tensor setting. The proposed scheme retains the high-order accuracy of semi-Lagrangian methods, ensuring stability for large time steps and avoiding dimensional splitting errors. The primary contribution of this paper is the novel extension of the algorithm from the matrix to the high-dimensional tensor setting, which enables the simulation of Vlasov models in up to six dimensions. The key technical components include (1) a third-order high-dimensional polynomial reconstruction that scales as $O(d^2)$, providing a point-wise approximation of the solution at the foot of characteristics in a semi-Lagrangian scheme; (2) a recursive hierarchical adaptive cross approximation of high-order tensors in a hierarchical Tucker format, characterized by a tensor tree; (3) a low-complexity Poisson solver in the hierarchical Tucker format that leverages the FFT for efficiency. The computed adaptive rank kinetic solutions exhibit low-rank structures within branches of the tensor tree resulting in substantial computational savings in both storage and time. The resulting algorithm achieves a computational complexity of $O(d^4 N r^{3+\lceil\log_2d\rceil})$, where $N$ is the number of grid points per dimension, $d$ is the problem dimension, and $r$ is the maximum rank in the tensor tree, overcoming the curse of dimensionality. Through extensive numerical tests, we demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed algorithm and highlight its ability to capture complex solution structures while maintaining a computational complexity that scales linearly with $N$.
item.dc:creator: Nanyi Zheng, William A. Sands, Daniel Hayes, Andrew J. Christlieb, Jing-Mei Qiu

item.title: Deep Learning of Solver-Aware Turbulence Closures from Nudged LES Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2604.23874v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The differentiable physics paradigm may be leveraged as an a-posteriori approach for discovering turbulence closure models by embedding a neural network parameterization directly inside the solver and optimizing it given potentially sparse target data. This addresses a key limitation of a-priori learning where direct numerical simulation (DNS) data is used to approximate the subgrid stress with the assumption of a low-pass filter. Closures trained in this a-priori manner frequently lead to unstable deployments due to the mismatch between the assumed filter and the effect of numerical discretizations and coarse-graining. In comparison, while typically stable during deployment, a-posteriori learning incurs high computational costs due to the need to backpropagate through a large eddy simulation (LES) solver. Furthermore, a-posteriori methods are challenging to apply broadly since they require significant modification of existing solvers. Finally, both approaches are limited when generalization is desired across different numerical schemes with their implicit filtering characteristics. In this work, we present a deep-learning approach for turbulence closure modeling built on the continuous data assimilation framework. Our approach enables the a-priori training of closures using DNS data observed only at coarse-grid points without modifying or differentiating through the LES solver, while preserving stability during deployment for the recovery of long-term statistics. We focus on the model's ability to adapt to different discretizations by explicitly conditioning it on the numerical scheme. We use two- and three-dimensional canonical cases to test our framework and show that the learned correction systematically tracks the discretization error of the coarse solver.
item.dc:creator: Ashwin Suriyanarayanan, Dibyajyoti Chakraborty, Romit Maulik

item.title: Tracking low-velocity ejecta from the DART impact on Dimorphos
item.description: arXiv:2606.15459v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The DART impact on Dimorphos produced a large population of low-velocity ejecta (v < vesc), likely containing most of the excavated mass, whose early fate remains poorly constrained. We investigate the first 22 h evolution of ejecta launched at 1-9 cm/s and assess how orbital dynamics and surface transport after first contact shape the surface distribution of the re-accreted ejecta blanket. We use RAVEL, a model that couples three-dimensional orbital dynamics in the Didymos-Dimorphos system with surface transport on a digital terrain model, including detachment, re-impact, rebound, and frictional sliding. Re-accretion is rapid and asymmetric: more than 99% of the re-accreted mass returns to Dimorphos within 5 h. The slowest ejecta remain concentrated near the DART crater and dominate the primary ejecta blanket, whereas faster particles undergo orbital transport and preferentially populate antipodal and trailing regions. Surface motion strongly modifies the first-contact pattern, and the DART-derived rough terrain model produces elongated, topographically channelled depositional streaks dominated by the slowest ejecta, giving rise to a ray-like pattern. These results provide testable predictions for ESA's Hera mission and link ejecta-blanket morphology to orbital dynamics, re-accretion, and surface topography.
item.dc:creator: Isabel Herreros, S\'ebastien Charnoz

item.title: Impact of Channel Dynamics on Higher-order Interactions of Oscillators
item.description: arXiv:2607.07662v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modeling higher-order interactions (HOIs) in nonlinear networks with static topologies is often physically restrictive. We demonstrate that standard 3-body Kuramoto couplings are mathematically equivalent to pairwise connections modulated by latent variables of transmission channels. While standard HOI topologies emerge in the adiabatic limit of these variables, relaxing this constraint reveals that latent channel timescales dictate collective macroscopic states. Specifically, transmission inertia drives bistability for symmetric interaction tensors and anti-phase cluster synchronization for antisymmetric ones. Furthermore, dynamically induced clustering in global topologies emerges as a finite-size effect of the dynamics of the local channels. Ultimately, we show that relying exclusively on static topologies restricts interaction modeling. Integrating latent variables captures the transient inertia and fundamental asymmetry of physical networks, bridging the analytical utility of higher-order functions with the reality of the underlying transmission medium.
item.dc:creator: Gabriel Marghoti, Isabela A. Martins, Giovana S. Spezzatto, Emanuel B. S. A. Cambraia, Sergio R. Lopes, Thiago L. Prado

item.title: Equivariant learning of a transferable three-dimensional classical density functional
item.description: arXiv:2608.13506v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Liquids exhibit collective behavior that depends sensitively on thermodynamic conditions, interfaces and confinement, yet predicting each new state commonly requires a separate atomistic simulation. Classical density functional theory offers a reusable variational description, but its central excess free-energy functional is generally unknown, and learned approximations for fluids have largely been developed in reduced-dimensional geometries. Here we show that this functional can be learned directly from fully three-dimensional canonical equilibrium density fields while preserving spatial symmetry and variational consistency, without free-energy or chemical-potential training labels. A functional learned from coarse three-dimensional density fields remains predictive at finer resolution, separating the sampling demands of training from the spatial resolution of subsequent predictions. A single learned functional transfers across temperatures, system sizes and statistical ensembles, and recovers the equation of state, liquid--vapor coexistence and interfacial broadening, none of which are used as training targets. Applied to complex three-dimensional geometries, it predicts the potential of mean force between colloids due to solvent mediation, and adsorption isotherms in an interconnected gyroid pore. These results demonstrate that molecular dynamics equilibrium density data can be converted into a transferable thermodynamic generator connecting microscopic liquid structure to response, phase behavior and collective phenomena.
item.dc:creator: Bingqing Cheng

item.title: Direct, Collision-Operator-Free Simulation of Electron-Ion Transport in Magnetized and Unmagnetized Plasmas
item.description: arXiv:2608.24012v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Accurate electron-ion collision models are central to predicting transport in fusion and space plasmas, yet collision operators and Monte Carlo collision models assume that a charged particle meets one partner at a time and that its successive encounters are independent. However, an electron that turns back along the magnetic field passes the same ions again. We solve the Newton-Lorentz equations for test electrons among static ions with a prescribed Debye-screened potential. The method combines force summation within an interaction radius, a time-symmetric particle pusher, and adaptive time stepping, enabling stable and scalable simulations in unmagnetized and magnetized plasmas. Using simulation-based measures of momentum relaxation and cross-field diffusion, we compare the simulations with a reference in the same model that treats every encounter as independent. Without a magnetic field the scattering rate reproduces the binary-collision rate for the same potential to within 2%. When the gyroradius is smaller than the Debye length, the scattering rate stays within 10% of the reference, but the cross-field diffusion coefficient exceeds it by a factor that grows with the field, up to 17. The excess comes from repeated passes of the same ions, whose guiding-center displacements add up: when the ions are replaced by new random ones many times per scattering time, so that a returning electron meets different ions, most of the excess disappears. The framework therefore provides a computational benchmark for testing and improving reduced collision operators and transport models.
item.dc:creator: Keheng Zhu, Jian Liu, Chaozhou Mou, Senran Lin, Wei Zhang

item.title: Scaling Density Functional Theory with Gaussian Splatting
item.description: arXiv:2609.31483v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Density functional theory (DFT) strikes a practical balance between accuracy and computational cost in many problems of computational chemistry and materials science. However, many DFT calculations are limited by fixed atom-centered basis sets, which dictate how accuracy and cost scale with system size. We propose Gaussian Splatting for Density Functional Theory (GS-DFT), which represents molecular orbitals as a cloud of Gaussians whose positions, shapes, and mixing coefficients are optimized jointly by gradient descent to minimize the energy without training data. Conceptually, GS-DFT is 3D Gaussian splatting with the renderer replaced by quantum mechanics. We introduce two key solver components: adaptive density fitting with screening for efficient evaluation of two-electron integrals, and a regularized differentiable orthogonalization of the molecular orbitals. Empirically, the optimized basis reaches the accuracy of the largest conventional basis sets with a fraction of the parameters, converging systematically in energy, density, and nuclear forces. At equal parameter count, it captures the stretched-bond and anion physics that fixed bases only recover with specialized basis augmentation. The resulting solver exhibits quadratic peak memory scaling in the cloud size, allowing us to simulate systems of up to 2,742 atoms (10,406 electrons) without any modifications at triple-zeta scale using a single four-GPU node.
item.dc:creator: Andr\'es Guzm\'an-Cordero, Cindy Zhang, Majdi Hassan, Marta Skreta, Kirill Neklyudov, Matija Medvidovi\'c

item.title: A time-domain adversarial example demonstrating the failure of $H^1$ elements in $a$-$\phi$ electromagnetic simulation
item.description: arXiv:2611.26546v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Frequently, $H^1$ continuous finite elements are used in computational electromagnetics despite it being widely known that such an interpolation is not guaranteed to furnish reliable approximations of solutions to general initial/boundary value problems. It is mathematically more natural to use $H(\text{Curl})$ elements (edge elements) than $H^1$ elements, since the former form part of a discrete complex that respects the differential-geometric structure of Maxwell's equations while the latter do not. However, most work discussing the failure of $H^1$ elements for electromagnetics is esoteric and concrete examples demonstrating the clear advantage of edge elements are generally restricted to quasi-static, frequency-domain, or eigenvalue problems. In this work, we summarize essential facts regarding $H^1$ and $H(\text{Curl})$ elements and present a physically feasible yet intentionally adversarial time-domain eddy-current example demonstrating the failure of gauge-penalized $H^1$ elements in an $a$-$\phi$ formulation compared to explicit gauge-free mixed scalar/edge $H^1/H(\text{Curl})$ elements. The results indicate that edge elements can be used to furnish reasonable results for general loading conditions, whereas penalized $H^1$ elements fail (e.g., converge to an incorrect state) even with mesh refinement.
item.dc:creator: Timothy Carlson, Sanjay Govindjee

item.title: High-Accuracy Neural-Network Quantum States via Randomized Real-Time Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2611.26587v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Neural-network quantum states (NQSs) exhibit a disparity in converging to the ground state during energy minimization: while the energy converges quadratically with the error in the variational wave function, other observables converge only linearly, which limits the accuracy of physical predictions. Here we show how to close this gap by introducing a new algorithm that improves the accuracy of NQSs. Our method, termed dynamical averaging, estimates expectation values by averaging over a state (or observable) evolved in real-time. Using insights from quantum information, we prove an up-to-quadratic suppression of error in arbitrary ground state observables, thus matching the fast convergence of the energy. Importantly, this improved accuracy requires neither further energy minimization nor increased model complexity, but rather exploits the effect of randomization on quantum states. We demonstrate dynamical averaging on non-integrable spin models, where it accelerates convergence and substantially reduces errors in observables.
item.dc:creator: John M. Martyn, Rod Rofougaran, Samuel Stein, Di Luo
